opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think that result is interesting, but I want to be careful about how much we read into it.

The intuitive story is that child-directed speech is simpler. The sentences are shorter, the vocabulary is more restricted, there's a lot of repetition, and the constructions are fairly canonical. So the model gets a cleaner signal about basic syntactic regularities, like agreement or word order, and it doesn't get distracted by everything that comes with Wikipedia or web text. That text has long, convoluted sentences, rare named entities, tables, boilerplate, and so on. There's a kind of curriculum argument here: maybe the input children get is well suited to learning, and maybe that's not an accident.

But there are a few caveats. First, faster isn't the same as better in the limit. At some point you need the complexity of adult language to learn the full grammar, and a model trained only on child-directed speech plateaus on certain constructions. Second, it matters what you evaluate on. If your syntactic benchmarks consist mostly of short, simple sentences, a model trained on short, simple sentences has a home-field advantage. Third, "Transformer" isn't one thing. The size of the model, the tokenization, and the training details can all interact with the domain of the data.

The bigger reason I care about this is that it bears on the poverty of the stimulus debate. If we want to argue about what's learnable from the input children actually receive, we should train on something like that input, in roughly that quantity, rather than on billions of words of internet text. The finding that the data is helpful in some respects is encouraging for that program. At the same time, in our own work we've found that even with child-like input, models don't necessarily generalize the way children do on things like hierarchical structure in question formation. So I'd say child-directed speech is a useful kind of data, but it doesn't by itself close the gap between how these models learn and how kids learn.

r002.rationale: It says child-directed speech is simpler and provides a cleaner signal for learning syntactic regularities than more complex Wikipedia or web text.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so I want to be careful about how I frame that, because it's one of those results that sounds more dramatic than it is, and I think the honest version is actually more interesting.

The setup was pretty simple. We took the same architecture, same training procedure, and we varied only the data: transcripts of speech directed at children, which is the CHILDES corpus, versus Wikipedia, versus a web crawl sample. Then we tracked, over the course of training, when the model starts getting things like subject-verb agreement right, when it handles relative clauses, those kinds of targeted syntactic evaluations. And the finding was that per token, the child-directed speech model acquired those generalizations earlier.

Now, the first thing I'd say is that "faster" there means more sample-efficient, not better in any absolute sense. If you keep training the Wikipedia model, it catches up and in many cases surpasses, because Wikipedia simply has more varied and more complex syntax in it. The child-directed data runs out of things to teach you fairly quickly. So this is not a claim that you should train your language model on baby talk.

What I think it does tell us is something about the structure of the learning problem. Child-directed speech has short sentences, a lot of repetition, a very constrained vocabulary, and crucially, the syntactic dependencies tend to be local. The agreement relation between a subject and a verb is usually one or two words apart. So the model can latch onto the pattern without having to simultaneously solve the problem of figuring out which of the fifteen intervening nouns is the one that matters. In Wikipedia, the first time you see a dependency, it's often buried in a sentence with three embedded clauses and a parenthetical about a Hungarian count. The signal is there but it's diluted.

And that connects to a much older idea in developmental psychology, this "less is more" hypothesis from Elissa Newport, that children might learn language well partly because of their limitations, not despite them. If you can only hold a few words in memory, you're forced to find local regularities first, and those turn out to be the right building blocks. Our result is weak evidence that something similar operates for these models: a curriculum that starts simple gets you to the basic generalizations sooner.

Where I'd push back on over-interpreting it is on the question of whether this says anything about human learning. Children get maybe a few million words a year. Our models, even the "small" ones, see orders of magnitude more than a child does by the age they've mastered agreement. So even the data-efficient condition here is nowhere near the human regime. What the result does is narrow the gap a little, and more importantly, it gives us a knob. We can ask: what properties of the input are actually doing the work? Is it sentence length? Is it the repetition? Is it the fact that conversational speech has a different distribution of constructions? Those are questions we can answer by manipulating the data, which is something you can't do with children.

So I'd put it as: it's a nice existence proof that input distribution matters a lot for the order and speed of acquisition in these systems, and it opens up a way of using them as a tool for asking questions about learnability. It's not a vindication of the idea that transformers learn like children. I'd be very surprised if that turned out to be true in any deep sense.

astra-6.text:
I think it suggests that the kind of language you learn from matters, not just how much of it you get. Child-directed speech tends to have shorter sentences and more repetition, and those properties may make it easier for a model to pick up grammatical patterns. So if we’re asking how much data a model needs to learn syntax, we shouldn’t assume that a word of Wikipedia is equivalent to a word of speech addressed to a child.

But I’d be careful about drawing conclusions about children from that result alone. A Transformer learning from transcripts isn’t in the same situation as a child interacting with a caregiver. The interesting next question is what accounts for the advantage: is it vocabulary, sentence complexity, repetition, or some combination? That would help us understand which properties of the input make learning easier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it suggests that the kind of input we give a model matters a lot, not just how much input we give it. Child-directed speech tends to have shorter sentences and more repetition, so it may make certain grammatical patterns easier to pick up. If you’re learning from Wikipedia, you’re encountering much more complicated material right from the beginning.

But I’d be cautious about drawing a direct conclusion about how children learn. We’re still talking about a Transformer, with a very different learning setup. What’s interesting is that data that looks more like children’s experience can help even this kind of model learn syntax more efficiently. That gives us a reason to study the structure of the input more carefully, rather than assuming that more internet text is always the best route.
